issue: When a jury's special interrogatory finds drug quantity below a mandatory-minimum threshold, may the sentencing judge find a higher quantity by a preponderance of the evidence, or is the jury's answer an affirmative finding of the actual amount that binds the court?

sides.position: The jury's special-interrogatory answer is an affirmative finding of the actual drug quantity attributable to the defendant, and the sentencing judge may not contradict it by finding a larger amount.
cases: United States v. Pimentel-Lopez, 859 F.3d 1134 (9th Cir. 2017)

sides.position: The jury's answer is at most an acquittal on the greater amounts, so the sentencing judge may find a higher drug quantity by a preponderance of the evidence despite the jury's special-interrogatory finding.
cases: United States v. Smith, 751 F.3d 107 (3d Cir. 2014)
United States v. Webb, 545 F.3d 667 (8th Cir. 2008)
United States v. Magallanez, 408 F.3d 672 (10th Cir. 2005)
United States v. Leontaritis, No. 19-40498 (5th Cir. 2020)

this_court: The majority takes the second position, holding that the jury's verdict on the special interrogatory does not bind the sentencing judge's drug-quantity finding. The dissent argues the majority joins the wrong side of the split.
quote: On the other side lie the Third, Eighth, Tenth, and, now, Fifth Circuits.
cite: United States v. John Leontaritis, No. 19-40498 (5th Cir. 2020)
